title: Feeling Management
outcomeStatement: By the end of this, you'll be able to name what you're feeling before it drives what you do.

practices.title: The last one that got away from you
practices.body: Think of the most recent time you reacted in a way you didn't choose. Write three sentences: what happened, what you did, what you wish you'd done. No analysis yet — just the facts.

practices.title: Your body knows first
practices.body: Today, watch for the physical change that arrives before the feeling does — the jaw, the shoulders, the stomach, the held breath. Don't fix it. Just catch it happening.

practices.title: What do you do with a feeling you don't want?
practices.body: Not what you should do. What you actually do — the honest mechanism.

practices.title: Your three reliable triggers
practices.body: Write the three situations that most dependably set you off. Be specific — not "work stress" but "being interrupted mid-sentence in a meeting". Specific is what you can see coming.

practices.cue: Before replying to anything that stings
practices.behavior: one full breath, all the way out
practices.title: One breath before the reply
practices.body: The gap between feeling and acting is where every other skill in this journey lives. This is the smallest possible version of it.

practices.title: Who gets which version of you
practices.body: Today, notice who gets your patient version and who gets the sharp one. No conclusions. Just count.

practices.title: What surprised you about what you saw this week?
practices.body: You've spent seven days watching instead of fixing. Look back at what you wrote.

practices.title: Rewind the tape
practices.body: Pick one flare-up from the past week. Write what happened in the thirty minutes before it. Most reactions are already loaded before the trigger arrives.

practices.title: What feeling are you least willing to be seen having?
practices.body: Take your time with this one. The answer is usually not the first one that arrives.

practices.title: What you reach for
practices.body: Today, notice what your hand goes to when a feeling arrives that you don't want — the phone, the fridge, the tab, the joke. Just see it.
practices.noticeFor: reaching for something instead of feeling it

practices.title: The same story, their side
practices.body: Take the flare-up from day 8 and write it as the other person would tell it. Not a fairer version — their version. You don't have to agree with it.

practices.title: Which feeling in you is usually covering another one?
practices.body: Anger is often the loud one standing in front of something quieter.

practices.title: The sentence you didn't say
practices.body: Think of a recent moment you softened or swallowed something. Write the direct version — one sentence, what you actually needed. You're not sending it. You're finding out whether you can write it.

practices.title: What have you learned about what your feelings are usually about?
practices.body: Two weeks in. Read back over what you've written before you answer.

practices.title: Count your words
practices.body: Write down every word you actually use for feelings — the ones that come out of your mouth, not the ones you'd find in a list. Count them. Most people have fewer than ten.

practices.title: Energy and pleasantness
practices.body: Draw two axes: energy high to low, pleasantness high to low. Place your last week's strongest moods in the four quadrants. Notice which quadrant you live in and which one you avoid.

practices.title: Two words instead of one
practices.body: Three times today, when you notice a feeling, name it in two words rather than one. Not "bad" — "tired and unappreciated". Precision is the skill.

practices.title: When you say you're fine, what are you usually actually?
practices.body: There's probably more than one answer, depending on who's asking.

practices.behavior: one sentence: the strongest feeling today, and what it was about
practices.title: One sentence before sleep
practices.body: Naming it once a day builds the vocabulary faster than anything else in this journey.

practices.title: Go back and relabel it
practices.body: Open what you wrote on day 1 — the reaction that got away from you. Rewrite the feeling using the more precise words you have now. Notice whether the event looks different.

practices.title: What changed when you got more precise?
practices.body: Look at the difference between how you described things in week one and how you describe them now.

practices.title: Write it, don't send it
practices.body: Pick something you softened recently. Write the honest version in full — the whole thing, unedited. Then close it. This is practice in saying it, not a decision to say it.

practices.title: Who taught you which feelings were allowed?
practices.body: Most people learned the rules early and have never looked at them since.

practices.title: Tell one person
practices.body: Say out loud, to one person you trust, the feeling you've been managing alone. You don't need them to fix it. Saying it is the whole practice.

practices.title: The gap
practices.body: Today, notice the space between feeling something and acting on it. Some days it's a second. Some days it's longer than you'd think. Just measure it.
practices.noticeFor: the gap between feeling and acting

practices.title: Your two that actually work
practices.body: Of everything you do to settle yourself — walking, breathing, calling someone, writing, leaving the room — write the two that genuinely work for you, and the specific situation each one is for. Two you'll use beats ten you won't.

practices.title: One real situation, on purpose
practices.body: Today, in one real moment where you'd normally react automatically, use the gap. Then write what you did instead — and whether it worked. Both answers are useful.

practices.title: That first reaction — what would happen now?
practices.body: On day 1 you wrote about reacting in a way you didn't choose. Read it again. Then answer: if that exact thing happened this afternoon, what would be different?
